tool_registry.What does a tool registry own in an agen: Tool names, schemas, handlers and validation. It is the single source of truth for what tools exist and how to call them.
tool_registry.Why keep it provider-neutral?: Different providers (OpenAI, Anthropic) have different tool-call formats. A neutral core with adapters avoids lock-in.
tool_registry.How do you validate arguments against th: Check required fields, types and enums, and reject unknown fields if strict. Use JSON Schema or a small validator.
tool_registry.How do you handle duplicate names and un: Reject a duplicate registration loudly. This exercise also rejects an unknown name with an error; the agent runtime above it can turn that into a message the model can read.
tool_registry.How do you report invocation errors?: As a structured error result (type, message) returned to the agent, keeping the loop alive.
tool_registry.Strict schema validation versus lenient: Strict catches bugs and injection early but rejects near-misses. Coercion is friendlier but can hide mistakes.
tool_registry.How do you version tools without breakin: Version the names or schemas, keep the old versions for a while, and make changes additive.

budgeted_agent_loop.What limits should an agent loop enforce: Maximum steps, tokens, wall time, retries and cost. Every loop needs a guaranteed stop.
budgeted_agent_loop.Why must the loop be deterministic for t: Tests need repeatable outcomes. Inject the clock, randomness and model responses.
budgeted_agent_loop.How do you separate retryable from perma: Classify by exception type or status code: timeouts and rate limits are retryable; validation or permission errors are permanent.
budgeted_agent_loop.How do you enforce token, step and time: Check every budget before each step and stop at the first one exceeded, recording which one.
budgeted_agent_loop.What goes in the trace?: Each step's action, result, error, tokens used, timing and the stop reason.
budgeted_agent_loop.Retry with backoff versus failing fast?: Backoff recovers from transient failures but adds latency and cost. Fail fast for permanent errors or tight budgets.
budgeted_agent_loop.What happens to partial tool side effect: They may be half-applied. You need idempotent tools, compensation, or at least a record of what ran.

supervisor_orchestration.What is supervisor-worker orchestration: A supervisor splits a goal into tasks and routes them to specialized workers, then collects and combines the results.
supervisor_orchestration.How are tasks routed by capability?: Match each task's required capability to the workers that declare it, with deterministic tie-breaking.
supervisor_orchestration.How do you schedule independent tasks an: Run tasks with no dependencies concurrently, gather the results, and feed dependent tasks when their inputs are ready.
supervisor_orchestration.How do you checkpoint and resume after a: Persist the state of completed tasks. On resume, skip them and rerun only the unfinished ones.
supervisor_orchestration.How do limits and the message bus intera: Limits (concurrency, rounds, budget) bound how many messages flow. The bus records the messages for tracing and replay.
supervisor_orchestration.Supervisor pattern versus a single agent: A supervisor adds modularity and parallelism but also coordination overhead and error propagation. One agent is simpler to debug.
supervisor_orchestration.What failure modes appear with many work: Duplicated work, conflicting outputs, cascading failures, cost blowups and context loss between agents.

context_compaction.Why does an agent need context compactio: The context window is finite, and long histories raise cost and latency. Compaction keeps the useful parts within the budget.
context_compaction.What must never be dropped?: The system prompt, the current task, recent messages and unresolved tool call and result pairs.
context_compaction.How do you choose which messages to summ: The oldest middle messages that are no longer active, keeping the head and the recent tail verbatim.
context_compaction.How do you keep tool call and tool resul: Treat a call and its result as one unit: never keep one without the other.
context_compaction.How do you enforce both the total and th: Check the summary against its own cap and the total against the budget, and truncate the summary if needed.
context_compaction.Summarization versus truncation versus r: A summary keeps meaning but is lossy. Truncation is cheap but blind. Retrieval keeps everything but needs a search step.
context_compaction.How can compaction lose information that: Exact values (ids, numbers, file paths) or constraints stated early can get summarized away. Tag must-keep facts.

tool_call_dag.Why run dependent tool calls as a DAG?: Some calls need others' outputs. A DAG runs independent calls in parallel and dependent ones in order.
tool_call_dag.What is a round?: A set of calls whose dependencies are all completed, run together before the next set.
tool_call_dag.How do you find calls whose dependencies: Track remaining dependency counts or check that every dependency is done. Topological order, as in Kahn's algorithm.
tool_call_dag.How do you enforce max_parallel?: Take at most max_parallel ready calls per round, in input order as this exercise specifies, and defer the rest to the next round.
tool_call_dag.How do you detect cycles and missing dep: Before running anything, check that every dependency names a known call, then run Kahn's algorithm on the graph: if it cannot order every call, there is a cycle.
tool_call_dag.What happens downstream when one call fa: Mark calls that depend on it (transitively) as skipped or failed. Do not run them.
tool_call_dag.Parallel rounds versus a fully async sch: Rounds wait for the slowest call. A fully async scheduler starts each call as soon as its inputs are ready.

tool_call_stream_parser.Why parse tool calls from a stream inste: Lower latency: show text and start tool execution earlier. Also enables UI streaming of the arguments.
tool_call_stream_parser.What makes streaming parsing hard?: Tags and JSON can be split anywhere across chunks, and you must not emit text that later turns out to be a tag.
tool_call_stream_parser.How do you handle a tag split across chu: Hold back any suffix that could be a prefix of the opening tag until the next chunk resolves it.
tool_call_stream_parser.How do you buffer text versus tool-call: Stream text outside tool tags immediately (minus a possible partial tag). Buffer everything inside the tags until the closing tag, then parse.
tool_call_stream_parser.What do you do with malformed JSON?: Emit an error event with the raw text rather than crashing or dropping it silently.
tool_call_stream_parser.Latency versus correctness when emitting: Emitting sooner lowers latency but risks showing text that is later reinterpreted. Hold back only what could be a tag.
tool_call_stream_parser.Structured tool-call APIs versus tag par: Structured APIs give reliable JSON with no parsing. Tag parsing works with any text model but is fragile.
